verdicts.note: About nine years as chief deputy plus appointed treasurer since July 2025 [S1][S3][S5]; he runs on continuity and staff retention [S5]. -1 rather than -2 is defensible because he has never won election to the office and the opponent is also a record candidate.

Thin but direction-correct: 'careful steward of the public's money', 'healthy reserves, responsible debt management' and no 'unnecessary financial burdens for future generations' [S5]. His clean-audit record [S1][S5] also leans toward the audit pole. With no concrete restraint proposals, -1 medium is the ceiling.

Runs on eight years as an elected commissioner managing budgets [S1][S5] and seven years as an appraiser [S4][S8]. Proven-record direction is correct. -1 medium fits a challenger with no time in the treasurer's office. Minor: the seven-years-as-appraiser claim in the basis rests on S4/S8, which are not among the cited sources.

Independent sources across a decade: the 2016 vote against unbudgeted positions and 'every budget is negotiable' [S6], the 2020 'the state must cut spending' with priority-based budgeting [S8], and the 2026 'cost effective' office pledge [S5] plus the campaign site [S3]. Supports -2 high.

The campaign site says he never voted to raise property taxes and led the admission-tax repeal [S3]. In 2020 he called a tax 'a slap in the face' [S8]. Two independent sources with a concrete repeal on the record support -2 high, even though the treasurer does not set taxes.

Kept a two-term pledge [S1][S3] and refused PAC, special-interest and lobbyist money in 2020 [S8]. +1 medium is right given the PAC refusal is undocumented this cycle. Minor: the basis says 'no current-cycle statement', but the term-limit claim does appear in the 2026 pamphlet [S1]; only the money pledge lacks a current statement.
